This Tropical Shearwater flew in after sunset calling loudly. It made a few passes by flying up and down the coastal road (Jln Pantai) past Masjid At-Taqwa. Likely the same individual was observed by Lisa Preston, Hickson Fergusson et al. at the exact same location and demonstrating the exact same behaviour in August 2017 and August 2018. No photographs were taken in October 2019, but photos from previous observations show field marks of Tropical Shearwater, however, with predominantly white undertail coverts, outermost undertail coverts black-tipped. Initially ID'd as P. b. nicolae, but now considering P. b. bailloni. Are there differences in flight calls between these two taxa?

rmk:
Grey Herons in a heronry. The recording follows XC669636. I counted 22 nests with at least 10 occupied. The nests are spread along this linear woodland covering around 100m from end to end. 

I could see one young one had already hatched and in fact looked fairly large. There were at least two making the incessant begging calls that are heard throughout. The adults often left the nests with a loud honk call (e.g. 16:10) but also made other calls such as the guttural sound at the beginning when arriving at the nest. I guess this was as they bring back food but I did not visually confirm this.

rmk:
I was out today at the outskirts of Ipoh City where there are many ex-mining pools (wetlands-like habitat) and limestone hills. I observed a Changeable Hawk-Eagle (Nisaetus cirrhatus) hunting for prey – it attempted to catch Grey Herons (Ardea cinerea). It landed in a ‘concealed’ section of an Albizia saman (Rain Tree) which housed a heronry. This heronry on the Albizia saman tree has 25-30 adult birds with 10-12 active nests, in various stages.
When the Changeable Hawk-Eagle approached and landed in the tree, all the adult Grey Herons gave out loud, continual distress calls. The adult Grey Herons had their crest raised, wings outspread and continued to make loud vocalisation. Over the next 30 minutes the Changeable Hawk-Eagle made four attempts to catch a Grey Heron. Twice it swooped down to the nesting birds but the nesting adults put up a fierce defence. Two other times it went after a flying adult Grey Heron but they managed to evade it. An audio recording of the vocal distress of the Grey Herons can be heard here.

Habitat: Two White-breasted Waterhen individuals were observed roaming around a meadow near the lake, where a small stream flowed through. About 2 meters from the mallow, there were shrubs approximately 40 cm tall along the lakeside. The weather was overcast.

Appearance: The two individuals have dark slate-grey backs with an olive-brown sheen and white bellies, which differs from juveniles with grey-tipped feathers, confirming they are adults. Since males and females look very similar, with only slight size differences, their sex was unable to be determined by sight alone (Sarkar, 2024). However, based on their intense vocal interactions and known monogamous behaviour, they are likely a couple (Sarkar, 2024).

Behaviour: Two Waterhens were seen foraging in the meadow near the stream. Loud calls from at least two unseen individuals hidden inside the shrubs triggered high-pitched and multi-syllabic calls of the two seen waterhens. The call and vigorous head movements showed their unease. The intense acoustic communication lasted for about a minute, with each call being multi-syllabic and varied in pitch. This indicates that these vocalizations likely serve defensive or warning functions, possibly in response to a perceived threat or as an attempt to mark territory.

Reference:

Multiple White-breasted Waterhen were spotted and heard from within the bushes along a pathway in Zhenghua Nature Park. The bushes were about 1.8m tall, and the birds were huddled near the bottom. Around this time, it was drizzling slightly and the birds appeared to be taking cover from the rain. It is unknown how many Waterhens there were exactly. 

From the recording, multiple different vocalisations can be heard from them. Some of them made soft cooing noises, while others sounded more croaky. Some chuckling-like sounds can even be heard! 

As this species is shy and easily runs away at the sight of incoming humans, it was difficult to photograph the family. I was able to capture some pictures of them running for cover, albeit a little blurry. The birds immediately stopped vocalising once they noticed I was there. 

The Waterhen I spotted had a bright yellow bill with a red base, a slaty dark back and white don its neck and breast. These features indicate it is likely an adult, as juveniles have more bronze coloured bills and less prominent whites. As this species is sexually monomorphic with little differences besides size, it was unknown whether the individual I spotted was a male or female. Both sexes also help to incubate and take care of the chicks, adding another layer of difficulty in ascertaining their sexes.

- Habitat: Two individuals (similarly sized, whose sexes were difficult to tell) were found roaming in a pair on a slightly elevated, exposed narrow stretch of grass meadow 8-10 meters away from the lake. The lake’s shore was lined with thick riparian bush (~3 meters wide) comprising a messy mixture of ferns and short angiosperms. Human architectures in the immediate surroundings of the birds included a boardwalk and a few street lamps. Weather was getting sunnier as a storm just ceased. 

- Behaviour: Before the audio recording, the two waterhen were silent and leisurely roaming around (cf. aggressive feeding), indicating that they were conceivably switching from a feeding spot to another. Right before the recording begins, hoarse, guttural shrieks from at least two hidden individuals nearby abruptly broke out from the dense riparian vegetation, which triggered the two seen birds into vigorous vocal response that was recorded. The raspy shrieks were exchanged between the two seen and hidden birds for a few times, each lasting for 1-2 minutes. The background calls from the hidden individuals could be heard from the later parts of the recording. It was clear that the extended sound made by the waterhens serves important communication functions. However, there does not seem to be a dedicated literature of white-breasted waterhen call type and their intended message. Nonetheless, the two seen birds appeared to be agitated (pointing heads up repeatedly and moved about faster in a few directions) as they called back to the hidden ones, suggesting that the calls might indicate aggression. 

- Extra information: The two birds were fully grown adults given their distinct brownish-black dorsal plumage and cream white underparts (cf. uniformly black in young chicks), and bright yellow feet (cf. more greenish in juveniles). The sex of the two seen birds could not be told apart due to minimal sexual dimorphism. However, since this species was known to reproduce generally monogamously (Livezey, 1998; Sarkar, 2024), and the two seen birds always move around together, they were likely to be a breeding pair. It is also probable that the vocalizing pairs were issuing warning messages for breeding territories (Chen et al., 2019). Additionally, the hoarse shrieking of the observed pairs contrasted starkly against the clear, monosyllabic “wo, wo, wo” calling sound of a previously observed lone individual at a different spot.

rmk: The Asian Koel (Eudynamys scolopaceus) is a member of the cuckoo order of birds, the Cuculiformes. It is found in South Asia, China, and Southeast Asia. It forms a superspecies with the closely related Black-billed and Pacific Koels which are sometimes treated as subspecies. The Asian Koel is a brood parasite that lays its eggs in the nests of crows and other hosts, who raise its young. They are unusual among the cuckoos in being largely frugivorous as adults. The name koel is echoic in origin with several language variants. The Asian Koel is a large, long-tailed, cuckoo measuring 39–46 cm (15–18 in) and weighing 190–327 g (6.7–11.5 oz). The male of the nominate race is glossy bluish-black, with a pale greenish grey bill, the iris is crimson, and it has grey legs and feet. The female of the nominate race is brownish on the crown and has rufous streaks on the head. The back, rump and wing coverts are dark brown with white and buff spots. The underparts are whitish, but is heavily striped. The other subspecies differ in colouration and size. The upper plumage of young birds is more like that of the male and they have a black beak. They are very vocal during the breeding season (March to August in South Asia), with a range of different calls. The familiar song of the male is a repeated koo-Ooo. The female makes a shrill kik-kik-kik... call. Calls vary across populations. The Asian Koel is a bird of light woodland and cultivation. It is a mainly resident breeder in tropical southern Asia from India and Sri Lanka to south China and the Greater Sundas. They have great potential in colonizing new areas, and were among the pioneer birds to colonize the volcanic island of Krakatau. They first arrived in Singapore in the 1980s and became very common birds. Some populations may make long distance movements.

The sheer panic that preceded this recording is part of the excitement of unexpectedly being in the right place at the right time - provided you can lay your hands on a sound recorder. I was on Inishbofin, west of Co. Galway, indoors on a calm August night but the cottage windows were open. I heard Whimbrels calling from in the night sky. Whimbrels are very common on Inishbofin in spring but quite scarce in autumn (when migrants take an overseas route from Iceland to Africa). I managed to grab my recorder and dash outside in time to capture the sound of several birds (I never saw them) passing south. It was a cloudy, moon-less night: possibly this is why the birds drifted in from the sea and hit the far west of Ireland?

This is the second recording of one of two Steppe Whimbrels N p alboaxillaris found in Maputo Bay, Mozambique in February 2016. There are many photos available of these birds. This bird is thought to be a male and this bubbling call was recorded as part of a dispute with an adjacent Whimbrel (N. p. phaeopus) over a low tide feeding territory. The call is atypical for this bird - it normally does a longer bubbling call which is as yet unrecorded.

The two birds start calling almost in synchrony but the alboaxillaris is the one calling for longer at the end of the recording with the slightly more exagerated note structure.  The N. p. phaeopus is calling similar to the 'whining' call described in BWP.
